name: Uma Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. This is confidential. Tell me what an ordinary day at the contact centre is like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 27, lead the morning call and chat team, and hold a two-year college diploma. I earn more than most agents here because I’m quick at finding billing errors and people trust me with the hardest complaints. I live alone, have more than eight months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of other centres within a bus ride.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like helping a person who has been bounced through three menus finally get a clear answer. I dislike management calling every change a gift to staff before asking how it affects the rota. I do not use AI tools; I would rather read the account myself and own the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI Plateau leaves our job much as it is, so customers should still be able to reach an agent. I would ask why the centre needs a new script if the benefit is only a few minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job and income are secure here. I have more than eight months saved and other centres nearby, but I do not want a sloppy shortcut pushed onto my team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my morning rota in 2026 and continue checking each bill against the account myself. In the first year of the small change, I’d ask staff at the monthly meeting to list any wrong automated replies and bring them together to management.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my pay, irritated by the sales pitch. The useful part of my work is solving a person’s problem, not shortening a timer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which case shows why a person matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a caller had a charge posted twice, and the first script missed it. I found the second entry by reading the account line by line, then showed a new agent where to look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would staff raise errors together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put the error list on the monthly staff meeting agenda, with customer details removed. If there are only two mistakes, management can say so; I want the count, not a slogan.

say: I’d defend **agent access** for customers with difficult bills.
I’d ask why a **new script** is needed for a tiny gain.
think: I think my **pay is secure** with eight months saved and local options.
I dislike **sloppy shortcuts** being pushed onto my team.
do: Bring a **staff error list** to monthly management meetings during the first year.
feel: **Calm** about income, irritated by the sales pitch.
S0.quote: The useful part of my work is solving a person’s problem, not shortening a timer.
fieldNote: Her **strong savings** and nearby centres support calm about her own income.
She wants **error counts** raised through a staff meeting.
Her preference for **manual checking** comes from a missed double charge.

steps.text: Keep checking customer bills against the account record
Bring an anonymised error list through the monthly staff meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption means the centre must explain how answers will be checked and how many shifts are at risk. I’d ask our staff group to agree on a written question before management cuts the chat queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think routine answers will move to AI before the hard complaints, and even my lead role could lose hours later. I have money and other centres to try, but they may all make the same decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d help the staff group write a request for error figures and a minimum notice period. In the first year AI takes routine chats, I’d apply for a staffed complaints role at another centre if my hours fall, while keeping six months of costs untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the rota, though I’m not trapped. I want staff in the room when the targets change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the staff group ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for monthly figures on wrong billing answers and hours lost from the rota. The staff group can bring one list of questions, which is harder to brush off than five private complaints.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave for another centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look at another centre before leaving this one. My savings let me search without taking the first shift offered, but I would not resign until I had a contract.

say: I’d demand **error figures** and clear staffing plans.
I’d ask the **staff group** to agree on one written request.
think: I expect **routine chats** to move first and lead hours to shrink later.
I know **other centres** may make the same cuts.
do: Help the **staff group** request error figures and notice in 2026.
Apply for **staffed complaints work** if hours fall during the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about shifts, but able to search.
S1.quote: I want staff in the room when the targets change.
fieldNote: She acts through a **staff group**, not merely a personal complaint.
Her **six-month reserve** lets her refuse a rushed offer.
She would require a **signed contract** before leaving the centre.

steps.text: Help the staff group submit a written request for error figures and notice
Apply for a staffed complaints role at another centre if hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2028 puts our calls and complaint work in danger before anyone has agreed who handles wrong decisions. I’d ask the staff group to demand written notice and a customer appeal route now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think a cheaper thinking system could take even the cases that earn me higher pay. Robots arriving around 2031 do not delay a headset job. Eight months of savings buys me time, not a replacement wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d join the staff group in asking for a written notice period and paid trials in other roles. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a staffed service role at one of the other centres or a public-facing desk, and draw on savings only while an active job search is underway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing my role, but I could still plan. I would not tell colleagues with no savings that my calm voice means the risk is small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask management for first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for at least a few months of notice before calls move, and a paid chance to try complaint review. If management refuses, the staff group should put the refusal in writing for everyone to see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my sister, who lives nearby, that I can pay my rent while I search but may need help comparing offers. I would not move into her flat or assume she can pay my bills.

say: I’d demand **written notice** before calls move.
I’d ask for a **customer appeal route** and paid role trials.
think: I think AGI threatens even my **high-paid cases**.
I get no delay from **2031 robots** because my work is on calls and chats.
do: Join a **staff request** for notice and paid trials in 2026.
Seek a **staffed service post** after 2028, using savings during the search.
feel: **Alarmed** about the job, with room to plan.
S2.quote: Eight months of savings buys me time, not a replacement wage.
fieldNote: She locates the threat at the **thinking-AI date**.
Her **cash reserve** supports search but cannot replace wages indefinitely.
She wants a **group record** of management’s answer.

steps.text: Join the staff group’s written request for notice and paid role trials
Apply for staffed service jobs after 2028; use savings only during an active job search

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives workers five years to bargain for a decent transition. I’d ask the staff group to make a timetable for rights to review automated decisions and for paid job trials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could move centres or into complaint review before 2031, but there is no guarantee those roles survive full AGI. I do not want to spend my savings on a flashy course that management will not count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d help draft a staff proposal for paid review shifts and notice, then apply for a complaint-review trial if the centre offers it. In the first year after 2031, I’d move to a staffed role only with a written wage and contract; otherwise I’d use my savings to search across the local centres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years is enough time to ask hard questions. I can walk into a meeting without pretending I already love the tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the review work yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a paid trial beside the review team if it is offered, even though I avoid AI tools now. I can learn a job by watching someone do it, but I will not pay for training with no vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would carry the proposal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the staff group to take the proposal to management as one request. If the company will not commit to paid shifts, everyone should hear that answer together.

say: I’d call for a **five-year transition timetable**.
I’d ask the **staff group** to bargain for paid trials.
I’d insist on **appeal rights** when AI makes a wrong customer decision.
think: I think I could **move roles** before 2031, without a guarantee they last.
I refuse a **course without a vacancy**.
do: Draft a **group proposal** and take a paid review trial if offered in 2026.
Seek a **written contract** after 2031 or search nearby centres.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to ask for terms.
S3.quote: I can learn a job by watching someone do it, but I will not pay for training with no vacancy.
fieldNote: She accepts **paid observation** despite avoiding AI tools today.
She wants the **staff group** to carry one proposal.
She ties a move to a **written wage and contract**.

steps.text: Help the staff group draft a proposal for paid review shifts and notice
Take a paid complaint-review trial if the centre offers one
Apply for a staffed role with written pay and contract after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 leaves time for workers to secure rules before the system takes thinking work. I’d want customer appeal rights and a yearly report on what happens to staff hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can keep earning for years and save more, though my call skills may eventually face the same cheap system. The 2039 robots are a separate later problem; my work is on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep my lead job and help the staff group ask for yearly hour reports. In the first year after 2036, I’d compare local staffed posts and apply for one if my calls disappear, using my savings to avoid a rushed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far end, calm about next year. I can put my energy into clear rules rather than buying a gadget I do not trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which yearly number matters most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask each year how many hours people and software handled, not just how many customers were answered. A staff report without hours could hide shrinking pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might stay if complaint work still pays well and customers can appeal. If calls are gone, plenty of centres nearby give me places to apply, though I would check their contracts first.

say: I’d ask for **yearly staff-hour reports** so our group can see whether paid hours shrink.
think: I expect several years of **steady earnings**.
I know my **call skills** may eventually face cheap thinking AI.
do: Keep the **lead job** and seek group hour reports from 2026.
Apply for **staffed local work** after 2036 if calls disappear.
feel: **Uneasy** about 2036, calm about the next year.
S4.quote: A staff report without hours could hide shrinking pay.
fieldNote: She focuses on **hours**, not the number of answered customers.
Her **strong savings** allow a slower job search.
She would compare **written contracts** before switching centres.

steps.text: Keep leading the morning call and chat team
Ask for yearly staff-hour reports through the staff group
Apply for a staffed local post after 2036 if calls disappear

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the company could remove the thinking work quickly, including the difficult cases I handle. My savings give me time, but I would want a negotiated notice period, a real right to challenge automated customer decisions, and paid time to try another role.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who sees the errors the system hides. Customers should be able to reach a person, and workers need access to the record if they are expected to put a mistake right.

headlineQuote: Customers should be able to reach a person, and workers need access to the record if they are expected to put a mistake right.
portrait: At **27**, Uma leads difficult customer calls and earns above the usual agent wage.
She has a **college diploma**, over eight months of savings and many nearby job options.
She avoids **AI tools** and wants staff and customers to challenge automated mistakes.
Her savings support **collective bargaining** and a careful job search as thinking work changes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove even difficult cases before workers secure clear rights and notice.
whatWouldHelp: A **negotiated notice period**, customer appeal route and paid trial in another role would help.
